annotations.keyFindings: Failure occurred in 31 percent of catheters before and 33 percent after the change to clinically indicated replacement, while catheters per 100 patient-days fell from 36 to 27 and median dwell rose from 58 to 81 hours.
annotations.limitations: Six-month periods on four surgical wards; ward records without adjustment for patient mix or other ward changes.

annotations.keyFindings: Monthly failure was 28 percent before the switch, with no step change (0.9 percentage points, -2.1 to 3.9) and no change in slope over 18 months on each side; a catheter brand change produced a short rise in occlusions.
annotations.limitations: Ward-level monthly counts; several catheters per patient not accounted for; one hospital.

annotations.keyFindings: Phlebitis did not rise with dwell beyond 96 hours (4.1 and 3.8 per 1,000 catheter-days), but site assessment was documented in 83 percent of shifts, least often at night and at weekends.
annotations.limitations: Three medical wards of one hospital; visual phlebitis scoring; too few bloodstream infections to study.

annotations.keyFindings: Routine resiting meant a median of three insertions per admission against two, and 38 percent against 24 percent of patients reported at least one insertion scored 7 or higher for pain.
annotations.limitations: Two hospitals with different patient mix; pain recorded only for observed insertions.

annotations.keyFindings: Among 812 catheters in patients aged 75 and over, infiltration occurred in 14 percent and became more frequent after the fourth day (hazard ratio 1.6 for each further day); infiltrations in patients with delirium were found later.
annotations.limitations: Two wards with higher than average nurse staffing; older patients only.

claims.text: After four surgical wards moved from routine to clinically indicated replacement, catheter failure occurred in 31 percent of catheters before and 33 percent after, in an unadjusted before-after comparison.
claims.passage: occurred in 31 percent of catheters before and 33 percent after
claims.interpretation: A planning value for the local comparison; unadjusted, so the small difference may reflect patient mix.

claims.text: On medical wards using clinically indicated replacement, phlebitis did not rise with dwell beyond 96 hours (4.1 per 1,000 catheter-days up to 96 hours and 3.8 afterwards), while site assessment was documented in 83 percent of shifts.
claims.passage: 4.1 per 1,000 catheter-days up to 96 hours and 3.8 per 1,000 catheter-days afterwards
claims.interpretation: Longer dwell need not mean more phlebitis where sites are scored every shift; documentation gaps are the weak point.

claims.text: In an interrupted time series over 18 months on each side of a switch to clinically indicated replacement, monthly catheter failure showed no step change (0.9 percentage points, 95 percent confidence interval -2.1 to 3.9) and no change in slope.
claims.passage: there was no step change at the switch (0.9 percentage points, 95 percent confidence interval -2.1 to 3.9) and no change in slope
claims.interpretation: A monthly series can separate a policy from trends; the same series showed a co-intervention (a catheter brand change).

synthesis: Five retrieved records from the first search, appraised at abstract level. After moves to clinically indicated replacement, catheter failure was similar in an unadjusted before-after cohort (31 and 33 percent) and showed no step change in an interrupted time series, insertions per patient fell, and phlebitis did not rise with dwell beyond 96 hours on wards that scored sites every shift. Infiltration rose after the fourth day of dwell in patients aged 75 and over. Patients reported less insertion pain where catheters were not routinely resited. None of the five examined bloodstream infection or accounted for several catheters per patient.
gradeRationale: Observational comparisons from single hospitals, mostly without adjustment for patient mix; broadly consistent in direction, serious risk of bias.
summary: Five retrieved records appraised; three source-derived claims; overall certainty low.
